newsitem.title: USA: Mayor says SEC probing Miami bond deal.
newsitem.headline: Mayor says SEC probing Miami bond deal.

text.p: The city of Miami, which recently saw top officials charged with corruption and is struggling with a record budget shortfall, is also the subject of a U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission probe into a $72 million pension bond issue, Mayor Joe Carollo said Thursday.
"The SEC has been around," Carollo told Reuters during a break in a city commission meeting.

He would not comment on reports that SEC officials had made informal requests for documents related to the taxable revenue bonds the city issued in December 1995. Carollo referred further questions to Acting City Manager Merrett Stierheim, who did not return Reuter calls.

Proceeds from the bond sale were to be used to meet pension fund obligations and to compensate retiring workers for unused sick leave. Questions about the use of the money arose last week when trustees for the City of Miami Firefighters and Police Officers Retirement Trust Fund said $37 million of bond proceeds were unaccounted for and may have been improperly co-mingled with general fund revenues.
After investigating, Stierheim said the money had been accounted for and used properly.

"There appears to be nothing irregular about the use of these bond monies," Stierheim said in a Sept 20 memo. However, the memo criticized the use of debt to meet current pension requirements, calling it "analogous to putting second and third mortgages on one's home."

The bond documents specified that some of the proceeds would be used to reimburse the city's general fund for its 1995 pension fund contribution. The issue was validated in court and no objections were raised during the appeals period that preceeded the sale.
SEC District Director Charles Senatore declined to comment.
The bonds were underwritten by Howard Gary & Co, which is also the city's financial adviser.

Carollo acknowledged the SEC probe during a break in a commission meeting that focused on the city's dire economic straits. Stierheim has said the city expects a budget shortfall for fiscal 1997, which begins Oct 1.
He was scheduled to disclose the amount of the shortfall and propose potential remedies at a city commission meeting Thursday night.
Carollo, who previously estimated the shortfall at $25 million, fall, saying, "The City of Miami is going through its worst financial crisis in its 100-year history."
The mayor said all city employees would be asked to "suck it in and give of themselves to the city," hinting that widespread salary cuts were pending.
"We're going to be asking everyone, I'm sure, to bite the bullet," said Commissioner Richard Dunn.
Miami was only able to balance the budget last year by laying off 600 workers and cutting $32 million of expenses.

The budget shortfall was discovered after the resignation of City Manager Cesar Odio, who was charged by federal prosecutors earlier this month with conspiring to solicit bribes in relation to city contracats.
City Commissioner Miller Dawkins was also charged in the bribery case, and prosecutors said former City Finance Director Manohar Surana had agreed to plead guilty on related charges.
Surana resigned in August, shortly before federal prosecutors revealed he had worn a hidden wire to record conversations implicating Odio, Dawkins and a well-known lobbyist.
